tips.title: Ecosystem includes the non-living
tips.body: A **community** is only the living things; an **ecosystem** is the community **plus** the soil, water, light and temperature. If a definition you write has no mention of non-living parts, it is a community, whatever you called it.

tips.title: If it is alive, it is biotic
tips.body: Competition, predation, disease and food are **biotic** because they involve organisms. Light, temperature, water, pH and wind are **abiotic**. One test settles every example: is it alive, or does it come from something alive?

tips.title: Random for how many, a line for how it changes
tips.body: **Random quadrats** estimate a **population**; a **belt transect** shows how distribution **changes across a gradient**. A transect is deliberately not random, so do not criticise it for that — it is the right tool for a different question.

tips.title: Mean per square metre, then times the area
tips.body: Convert the mean per quadrat to a **density per m²** first — divide by the quadrat area if it is not 1 m² — then multiply by the total area. Doing it in that order makes a 0.25 m² quadrat no harder than a 1 m² one.

tips.title: Name where the 90% went
tips.body: **Respiration as heat**, **egestion**, **excretion**, and **parts not eaten**. Saying *energy is lost* scores nothing on its own; the mark is for where it went, and there are four places.

steps.title: Levels of organisation
steps.body:
Ecology has its own ladder of terms, and using the wrong rung is an easy mark to lose. From smallest to largest:

- An **individual** — one organism.
- A **population** — all the organisms of **one species** in a habitat.
- A **community** — all the **populations of all the species** living in a habitat.
- An **ecosystem** — the community **together with the non-living parts** of the habitat, and the interactions between them.

The jump that matters is the last one. A community is **only the living things**; an **ecosystem includes the non-living** — the soil, the water, the light, the temperature. So a pond's community is the fish, plants and insects; the pond **ecosystem** is those plus the water, the mud and the sunlight falling on it.

Two more terms you need:

- A **habitat** is the place an organism lives.
- **Biodiversity** is the variety of different species in an ecosystem.

steps.title: Abiotic and biotic factors
steps.body:
Communities are affected by two kinds of factor, and the names are simply Greek for *without life* and *with life*.

**Abiotic factors — the non-living conditions:**

- light intensity
- temperature
- moisture, or water availability
- soil pH and mineral content
- wind intensity and direction
- carbon dioxide level (for plants) and oxygen level (for aquatic animals)

**Biotic factors — the effects of other living things:**

- **competition** — for food, water, light, space or mates
- **predation** — being eaten
- **disease** — pathogens spreading through a population
- the **availability of food**
- new species arriving and outcompeting the existing ones

A useful test: if the factor **is alive or comes from something alive**, it is biotic. Food is biotic; water is abiotic. Predators are biotic; temperature is not.

A change in one factor rarely affects only one species, because the species are connected — which is the subject of the next step.

steps.title: Interdependence, mutualism and parasitism
steps.body:
**Interdependence** means the species in a community **depend on one another** — for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal and more. Because of it, a change affecting one species can ripple through the whole community.

If a population of insects falls, the birds that eat them have less food, so the bird population falls too; the plants those insects pollinated set fewer seeds. Nothing in a community is affected alone.

Two particular relationships are named on the specification.

**Mutualism** — a relationship where **both** species benefit:

- **Oxpeckers** and large mammals: the bird eats ticks and parasites from the mammal's skin. The bird gets food; the mammal is cleaned.
- **Nitrogen-fixing bacteria** in the **root nodules of legumes**: the bacteria get sugars and a place to live; the plant gets nitrogen compounds.
- **Cleaner fish** and larger fish: the same arrangement, underwater.
- **Chemosynthetic bacteria** in **giant tube worms**: the bacteria get shelter and raw materials; the worm gets food.

**Parasitism** — one species, the **parasite**, **benefits while the other, the host, is harmed**:

- **fleas** on a mammal, feeding on its blood
- **head lice** on a human
- **tapeworms** in an intestine, absorbing digested food
- **mistletoe** on a tree, taking water and minerals

The distinction is simply **who benefits**: both, or only one at the other's expense.

steps.title: Core practical: quadrats and transects
steps.body:
**Core practical 9.5** asks you to investigate the relationship between organisms and their environment using **quadrats** and **belt transects**, and 9.6 asks you to work out numbers from the data.

**A quadrat** is a square frame of known area, placed on the ground, in which you count the organisms or estimate the percentage cover. Quadrats must be placed **randomly** if you are estimating a population — using random number pairs as coordinates on a grid — because choosing where to put them would bias the result towards the places you noticed the species.

**A belt transect** is a line across a habitat, along which quadrats are placed at regular intervals. This is **not** random, and deliberately so: a transect is used when you want to see how a species **changes across a gradient** — up a beach, or from a hedge into a field.

So the two techniques answer different questions: **quadrats placed randomly** estimate *how many*; a **transect** shows *how the distribution changes*.

steps.title: Energy through a food chain
steps.body:
This section is **Biology only** (spec points 9.7B and 9.8B).

At each step of a food chain, **only about 10% of the energy** is passed on to the next level. The rest is **transferred to less useful forms**, and you should be able to say where it goes:

- **respiration**, which releases energy as **heat** to the surroundings
- **egestion** — the parts that are not digested, lost in faeces
- **excretion** — waste such as urine
- parts that are **not eaten**, such as bones, roots or bark

That is why food chains are short: after four levels there is too little energy left to support another.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Define population, community and ecosystem, and say which includes the non-living parts.
2. Give three abiotic and three biotic factors.
3. What is the difference between mutualism and parasitism?

**Part B.**

4. Twelve 0.5 m² quadrats give a total of 48 plants. Find the mean per quadrat and per square metre.
5. Explain why quadrats must be placed randomly when estimating a population, and why a transect is not.
6. A trophic level holds 5000 kJ and the next holds 400 kJ. Calculate the efficiency.

**Part C.**

7. Explain why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels.
8. A pond's insect population falls sharply. Explain, using interdependence, how this could affect other species in the community.

For question 4, careful: the quadrats are **0.5 m²**, not 1 m², so the mean per quadrat is not the same as the number per square metre.

steps.title: Going deeper: humans, biodiversity and food security
steps.body:
**Human interactions, positive and negative.** Spec point 9.9 asks for both, and a good answer gives some of each rather than a list of harms.

*Negative:* **deforestation** removes habitats and reduces biodiversity; **pollution** from farming and industry poisons water and air; **building** destroys and fragments habitats; **overfishing** removes species faster than they can reproduce; **introducing species** that outcompete the natives.

*Positive:* **conservation schemes** and **nature reserves**; **replanting** hedgerows and woodland; **captive breeding** programmes for endangered species; **recycling** to reduce the demand for raw materials; **fishing quotas** so stocks recover.

**Why biodiversity matters** (9.10). Not for its own sake, but for what depends on it:

- A community with **more species** is **more stable**, because if one species declines others can fill its role. A community of few species can collapse when one fails.
- Species provide **resources** — food, medicines, materials — including ones not yet discovered.
- Ecosystems provide **services** that would be costly to replace: pollination of crops, decomposition, water cycling, and removal of carbon dioxide.

**Food security** (9.11B, Biology only) means having enough safe food for a population. The **biological** factors affecting it are the ones examined:

- **rising human population**, so more mouths
- **changing diets**, as wealthier populations eat more meat, which needs far more land and energy per kilojoule because of the 10% rule
- **new pests and pathogens** damaging crops and livestock
- **environmental change**, such as drought, affecting where crops grow
- **sustainability** of farming methods
- the **cost** of agricultural inputs

The meat point is the one to be able to explain rather than state: feeding grain to an animal and then eating the animal adds a trophic level, and **90% of the energy is lost** at it. Eating the grain directly feeds far more people from the same land.

**Indicator species** (9.16B, Biology only) are species whose presence or absence indicates pollution, and using them is worth **evaluating** rather than just describing.

- **Lichens** are sensitive to **sulfur dioxide** in air: many lichen species means clean air, few means polluted.
- **Freshwater shrimps** and **stonefly** nymphs need clean, well-oxygenated water; **bloodworms** and **sludgeworms** survive in **polluted** water.
- For air, as well as lichens, **blackspot fungus on roses** is sensitive to sulfur dioxide, so roses free of blackspot can indicate polluted air.

*For:* cheap, needs no equipment, and shows the **effect over time** rather than at one instant. *Against:* it is **qualitative** rather than precise; a species may be absent for another reason entirely, such as the wrong habitat; and it does not identify **which** pollutant. So indicator species are good for a first survey and poor for a legal measurement — which is the judgement a top answer reaches.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Population**: one species. **Community**: all the species. **Ecosystem**: the community **plus the non-living parts**.
- **Abiotic** factors are non-living — light, temperature, water, pH, wind. **Biotic** factors involve other organisms — competition, predation, disease, food.
- **Interdependence**: species depend on one another, so a change to one ripples through the community.
- **Mutualism**: **both** benefit — oxpeckers, cleaner fish, nitrogen-fixing bacteria in legume root nodules.
- **Parasitism**: the parasite benefits and the **host is harmed** — fleas, head lice, tapeworms, mistletoe.
- **Quadrats** are placed **randomly** to estimate a population; a **belt transect** follows a line to show how distribution **changes**.
- Population estimate = **mean per quadrat × total area ÷ quadrat area**.
- **Biology only**: about **10%** of energy passes to the next trophic level.
- The rest goes to **respiration as heat**, **egestion**, **excretion**, and parts **not eaten**.
- $\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{\text{energy transferred}}{\text{energy available}} \times 100$.
- Food chains are **short** because so little energy is left after a few steps.
- **Biodiversity** makes a community more **stable**, and provides resources and services.
- **Food security** is affected by population growth, diets shifting to meat, pests, environmental change, sustainability and cost.
- **Indicator species**: **lichens** and **blackspot fungus on roses** for air; **freshwater shrimps** and **stonefly** for clean water, **bloodworms** and **sludgeworms** for polluted. Cheap and long-term, but qualitative and not specific.

questions.prompt: A student estimates the number of dandelions in a 2000 m² field. They place ten 1 m² quadrats and count 4, 7, 5, 8, 6, 6, 5, 7, 4 and 8 plants. Calculate the estimated population, explain why the quadrats were placed randomly, and suggest how the estimate could be made more reliable.
questions.solution: The total number of dandelions counted across the ten quadrats is sixty. Dividing this by the ten quadrats gives a mean of six dandelions per quadrat. Since each quadrat has an area of one square metre, this is a density of six dandelions per square metre. Multiplying this density by the total area of two thousand square metres gives an estimated population of twelve thousand dandelions. The quadrats have to be placed randomly, for example by using pairs of random numbers as coordinates on a grid laid over the field, because if the student chose where to put them they would be likely to place them where they had already noticed dandelions growing, which would bias the estimate and make it too high. The estimate could be made more reliable by using a larger number of quadrats, because the mean is then less affected by any one unusually high or low square, and by making sure the quadrats are spread across the whole field rather than concentrated in one part of it.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The calculation.**

- Total: $4+7+5+8+6+6+5+7+4+8 = 60$
- Mean per quadrat: $60 \div 10 = 6$
- Each quadrat is 1 m², so the density is **6 per m²**
- Estimated population: $6 \times 2000 = \mathbf{12\,000}$ dandelions

Say **estimated**. It is a sample scaled up, not a count.

**Why randomly?** If the student chose where to place them, they would tend to pick spots where they had already **noticed** dandelions, biasing the estimate upwards. Randomness is achieved by laying a grid over the field and using **pairs of random numbers as coordinates**.

**Making it more reliable.** Use **more quadrats**: the mean is then less affected by any one unusually high or low square. Also make sure they are spread across the **whole** field rather than concentrated in one part.

Note that *more reliable* is about **repeatability**, which is why the answer is *more quadrats* rather than *count more carefully*.

questions.prompt: Explain why only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is passed on to the next, and explain what this means for the length of food chains and for the land needed to produce meat.
questions.solution: At each trophic level, only a small proportion of the energy taken in by an organism ends up stored in its body where it can be passed on when it is eaten. Much of the energy is used in respiration, which releases it as heat to the surroundings. Some is lost through egestion, because not all of the food eaten can be digested and the remainder is lost in faeces. Some is lost through excretion, in waste such as urine. In addition, parts of an organism such as bones, roots or bark are often not eaten at all, so the energy in them is never transferred. Taken together these losses mean that only about ten per cent of the energy is passed on. This explains why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels, because after a few steps so little of the original energy remains that it cannot support another level. It also explains why producing meat requires more land than growing crops for people to eat directly, because feeding grain to an animal and then eating that animal adds an extra trophic level, at which about ninety per cent of the energy is lost, so far fewer people can be fed from the same area of land.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Where the energy goes.** At each level, only a small part of what an organism takes in is stored in its body where it can be passed on:

- **Respiration** releases energy as **heat** to the surroundings.
- **Egestion**: not all food can be digested, and the rest is lost in **faeces**.
- **Excretion**: waste such as **urine** carries energy away.
- **Parts not eaten**: bones, roots and bark are often left.

Together these leave about **10%** to pass on.

**Why food chains are short.** Four steps of 10% takes 10 000 kJ to 1000, then 100, then 10 — a **thousandth** of the original. There is simply not enough left to support another level.

**Why meat needs more land.** Feeding grain to an animal and then eating the animal adds an **extra trophic level**, at which about **90%** of the energy is lost. Eating the grain directly feeds far more people from the same area.

The last point is the one worth being able to derive rather than recall: it follows from the 10% rule, and a question about food security is usually testing whether you can make that connection.

examTechnique.body:
Use the right word for the level of organisation. Population, community and ecosystem are not interchangeable.

For a quadrat calculation, find the mean per quadrat, convert to a density per square metre, then multiply by the total area. Show each step.

Call the result an estimate, and if asked how to improve it say more quadrats, spread across the whole area.

For energy transfer, give the equation, then name where the lost energy went. There are four routes and they carry marks.

When asked about human effects on ecosystems, give positive as well as negative examples. The specification asks for both.

When asked to evaluate indicator species, give what they are good for and what they cannot tell you.
examinerErrors: Defining an ecosystem as all the living things, which is a community.
Calling food or predation an abiotic factor.
Forgetting to divide by the quadrat area when it is not one square metre.
Saying energy is lost without naming where it goes.
Saying energy is destroyed, rather than transferred to less useful forms.
Saying mutualism is where one organism benefits.
Criticising a transect for not being random, when it is not meant to be.
Listing only harmful human effects when the question asks about interactions.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer keeps the levels of organisation straight and never uses ecosystem where community is meant. In a sampling calculation it converts to a density per square metre before scaling, so a quadrat that is not one square metre causes no trouble. It names all four routes by which energy is lost, and can then derive both the shortness of food chains and the land cost of meat from the 10% figure rather than recalling them as separate facts. Asked to evaluate indicator species, it gives the cost and time advantages, the qualitative limitation, and a judgement about when each matters.
